# Results — Study 626 (Unemployment-Trend-Timing, "Growth-Trend Timing")

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test
(Livingston / Philosophical Economics 2016, "Growth-Trend Timing") — **only obey the 200-day
SMA when unemployment is also rising**: the recession filter that supposedly halves
trend-following whipsaws. GTT goes risk-off **only** when (month-end close < 200d SMA) AND
(unemployment above its 12-month SMA); pure Faber timing (study
[110-faber](../../110-faber-timing/)) goes risk-off on the trend alone. Offline &
deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.
As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month). Fingerprint `a6195d69eb89`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Equity tape | S&P 500 **total return** = ^GSPC daily closes (yfinance, price-only index) + Shiller monthly dividend yield / 12; price-only leg kept as a robustness check |
| Window | 1949-02-28 → 2026-06-30 (**928** months, **77.3** years) |
| Unemployment | BLS **LNS14000000** (U-3, seasonally adjusted, monthly, 1948-01→2026-06), fetched once from the keyless BLS API v2 (same numbers as the `pub/time.series/ln/` flat file) |
| Cash | 3-month T-bill: ^IRX monthly mean from 1960; **1948–59 hardcoded annual averages** from the Economic Report of the President 2011, Table B-73 (constant within year — documented approximation) |
| Execution / lags | signals formed at the close of month *m* set the position for month *m+1* (**one** execution lag); the unemployment leg additionally honours the **1-month reporting lag** (the month-*m* rate is published in early *m+1*, so the signal uses the prior month's print) |
| Costs | **5 bps one-way × NAV** per switch headline; sweep 0/5/10/25 |

> **Vintage caveat (named on the Signal axis).** The unemployment series is the *current*
> vintage: seasonal factors and benchmark revisions have reshaped the historical path since
> the original real-time prints. A genuinely real-time backtest would have seen slightly
> different values near turning points. The reporting lag is modeled; the revision history is
> not (no free point-in-time vintage source in this sandbox).

## The race (net of 5 bps, total-return, Sharpe excess-vs-excess over the same cash)

| strategy | CAGR | vol | Sharpe | max DD | $1 grows to | switches | months out |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Buy & hold | 11.72% | 14.46% | 0.562 | −50.89% | $5,280 | 0 | 0.0% |
| Faber 200d SMA | 11.21% | 10.62% | 0.676 | −23.26% | $3,703 | 112 | 28.6% |
| **GTT (filtered)** | **12.59%** | 12.57% | **0.688** | −29.55% | **$9,610** | **60** | 13.7% |

## Whipsaws — the mechanical half of the claim

A **whipsaw** = a risk-off spell whose compounded cash-minus-equity P&L is negative (being
out lost money); a **save** = the exit dodged losses.

| rule | switches | risk-off spells | whipsaws | saves |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Faber | 112 | 56 | 44 | 12 |
| **GTT** | **60** | **30** | **16** | **14** |

Switches cut **46%**, whipsaw spells cut **64%** — the "halves the whipsaws" half of the
claim is **confirmed, and then some**, while every big save survives (GTT kept the full 2008
exit and 25 of Faber's 30 months out in 2000-02).

## Active-return inference (Newey-West HAC t on monthly active returns)

| pair | mean active | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|
| **GTT − Faber** | **+12.26 bps/mo** | **+2.32** |
| GTT − B&H | +4.37 bps/mo | +0.61 |
| Faber − B&H | −7.90 bps/mo | −0.88 |

Cost sweep on GTT − Faber (GTT trades *less*, so the edge **grows** with cost):
**t = +2.28 / +2.32 / +2.36 / +2.49** at 0/5/10/25 bps one-way.

**HAC lag sensitivity (named).** The active-return series is *negatively* autocorrelated
(acf1 = **−0.155**, itself ≈ 4.7σ from zero at n = 928 — whipsaw months reverse), so here
the Newey-West correction legitimately **shrinks** the standard error: plain (lag-0)
t = **+1.88**; HAC t = **+2.05 / +2.32 / +2.44** at 1/6/12 lags (the headline uses the
standard rule-of-thumb 6 lags). The stamp clears the bar at *every* lag choice ≥ 1; only
ignoring the serial correlation entirely drops it under 2.

## Exposure vs skill — the honest decomposition

GTT is long in **14.9%** of months where Faber sits in cash, and any filter with that duty
cycle mechanically collects the unconditional equity premium there:

| component | bps/mo |
|---|--:|
| GTT − Faber edge (net) | **+12.26** |
| mechanical exposure (14.9% × unconditional excess return) | +10.12 |
| pure timing (residual) | **+2.15** |

**Rotation placebo** (all **904** circular rotations of the `unemp_rising` series — same
persistence, same duty cycle, alignment destroyed; deterministic full enumeration): observed
**+12.26** vs rotation mean **+4.69** bps/mo, **p = 0.0509**. The filter's specific alignment
sits *exactly at* the 5% line — better than almost every fake filter of the same shape, but a
skeptic cannot quite reject "duty-cycle luck" at 5%.

## Robustness

| variant | GTT − Faber | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|
| unemployment SMA window 6m | +11.93 bps/mo | +2.30 |
| **12m (headline)** | **+12.26 bps/mo** | **+2.32** |
| 24m | +10.76 bps/mo | +1.96 |
| price-only tape (no dividends) | +8.11 bps/mo | +1.52 |

The 24-month window sits marginally under the bar; the price-only leg (which strips the
dividend income GTT's extra market time earns) drops to t = 1.52 — both named. Sub-period
(split at the Feb-2016 publication): pre **+10.46 bps/mo (t = 1.86)**, post
**+27.78 bps/mo (t = 1.64)** — the sign holds out-of-sample; each half alone is underpowered.

## The six bears — where the filter wins and where it fails

| episode | B&H | Faber (months out) | GTT (months out) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1974 bear | −11.2% | +38.0% (23m) | +14.8% (12m) |
| 1987 crash | −16.9% | −18.5% (5m) | −16.9% (0m) |
| 2000-02 bust | −25.1% | +13.1% (30m) | −9.2% (25m) |
| 2008 GFC | −22.7% | **+21.2% (19m)** | **+21.2% (19m)** |
| 2020 COVID | +18.4% | +14.2% (3m) | +13.0% (1m) |
| 2022 bear | −4.3% | −11.6% (9m) | **−4.3% (0m)** |

The filter keeps the classic recession saves (2008 identical to Faber; most of 2000-02) and
erases the 2022 whipsaw — but it is **blind to fast, non-recessionary crashes**: in 1987 and
March 2020 unemployment had not yet risen, so GTT rode the crash fully (its −29.55% max DD is
dated 1987-11). The shield is **regime-dependent by construction**: it only works when the
bear is a slow recession that shows up in the jobless rate first.

## Synthetic control — the machinery is honest

Two-regime world (expansion/recession), planted recession drag `gap` on equity returns; the
filter either tracks the true regime (`linked`) or an independent one (the null). The
**raw t is bait** — staying invested more always looks good when the premium is positive —
and the rotation placebo must refuse it:

| scenario | raw GTT−Faber t | rotation placebo p |
|---|--:|--:|
| planted drag, filter informative | +2.30 | **0.022** (fires) |
| null: filter is pure noise | −1.38 | 0.988 (quiet) |
| exposure-only bait (no drag planted) | **+2.23** | **0.586 (correctly refused)** |

The third row is the whole story: a filter with zero information produces a raw *t* above 2
purely by adding exposure, and the placebo correctly refuses it. *(Machinery proof only —
never cited in support of a stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — REAL.** Adding the unemployment filter to the 200-day SMA improved the rule by
  **+12.26 bps/mo** at **HAC t = +2.32** on 77 years of real tape, rising to **t = +2.49** at
  25 bps costs, robust to the filter window (6m/12m; 24m = 1.96), with whipsaw spells cut
  **64%** and switches **46%**. Named caveats: the tape is the **current vintage** of a
  revised macro series (reporting lag modeled, revisions not); the price-only leg reads
  t = 1.52; and most of the edge is mechanical exposure (next axis).
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Deployable by anyone (S&P fund + T-bills, ~0.8 switches/yr,
  edge survives 25 bps), but the edge over simply **buying and holding** is uncertified
  (+4.37 bps/mo, t = 0.61) and the crash protection is **regime-dependent**: blind to 1987-
  and 2020-style fast crashes, valuable only in slow, recessionary bears. A better Faber, not
  a certified money machine.
- **"Skill beyond exposure — or just more time in the market?" — MIXED.** Of the +12.26
  bps/mo, **+10.12 is mechanical exposure** any same-duty-cycle filter collects; the pure-
  timing residual is **+2.15 bps/mo** and the exposure-matched rotation placebo lands at
  **p = 0.0509** — the alignment beats ~95% of fake filters but misses the 5% line by a hair.
  The certified statement is "**the same or better, with half the trades and 64% fewer
  whipsaws**"; the stronger "the filter *times* recessions" is not quite certified.
